Spain has 17 regional governments with their own parliaments and presidents.

It was never meant to. The plan was three.

The story of how a single phrase — "coffee for everyone" — redrew Spain's internal map, a thread 🧵🗺️

1/ The 1978 constitution had to square a circle: guarantee "the indissoluble unity of the Spanish Nation" while recognising the "nationalities" inside it. Plural. The drafters made it work by never defining the word.

2/ Three regions expected special treatment — Catalonia, the Basque Country and Galicia. Each had its own language, each had autonomy under the 1930s republic, each had spent the Franco years with that language pushed out of public life.

3/ Then a minister from Seville, Manuel Clavero Arévalo, asked why Andalusia shouldn't get the same fast route to self-government. His answer became the nickname for the entire system: "café para todos" — coffee for everyone.

4/ So Spain didn't build three special cases inside a centralised state. It built 17 autonomous communities plus 2 autonomous cities, nearly all with parliaments and presidents. Andalusia voted for the fast track in February 1980 and took it.

5/ Which pleased almost nobody — and the genuinely unequal deals survived anyway. The Basque Country and Navarre still collect most of their own taxes and send Madrid a negotiated quota. Catalonia has never been given the same.
7/ That asymmetry is one of the quiet engines behind everything that followed in Catalonia: the struck-down 2006 statute, the illegal 2017 referendum, Article 155 and direct rule from Madrid.

Galicia, Andalusia, Aragon, the Canaries and more — the full map of the nations inside Spain, in this week's Lines & Legends, free every 3 days: https://buttondown.com/forummapping
